extracted.intended_audience: graduate students, researchers, and scholars in paleontology, macroevolution, and history/philosophy of evolutionary biology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual standards for building, testing, and interpreting models of extinction and diversification in paleontology (e.g., null/random models, mass-extinction explanations, species-as-particles simulations). Emphasizes when to invoke taxon-specific explanations versus stochastic/null hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Null model / randomness (Gambler’s Ruin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model extinction by treating species as particles with probabilistic origination/extinction (the 'field of bullets' idea). Under this null, extinction often results from chance rather than taxon-specific vulnerabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a species-as-particles stochastic model (Gambler’s Ruin analogy) where each species has a per-interval probability of extinction and speciation (e.g., 50/50 per million years). Interpret genus- or clade-level extinction as an absorbing boundary (analogous to gambler going broke). Do not attribute extinction to taxon peculiarities unless observed patterns deviate from the null expectations. The gambler analogy shows that even well-adapted groups can be destined for eventual extinction by chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare observed fossil patterns to null-model predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether actual extinction/origination patterns in the fossil record are consistent with what random-process null models predict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute probabilistic expectations from the null (e.g., expected time-to-extinction for a genus with N species) and compare observed durations/rates. If observed rates are consistent with the null, refrain from invoking adaptive/competitive explanations; if inconsistent (higher or lower), search for special causes that could explain the deviation. Example: if a genus with 10 species is expected to go extinct in 40 Myr under the null but some species persist 300 Myr, consider taxon-specific explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to invoke competitive / taxon-specific explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Only appeal to the peculiarities of individual taxa (Darwinian competition, adaptive superiority) when empirical data show deviations from null-random expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the null can generate many patterns traditionally attributed to selection, reserve adaptive/competitive explanations for cases where the fossil record is improbably different than stochastic predictions. The chapter emphasizes that Darwin lacked a null expectation and thus over-attributed extinctions to competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Van Valen’s Law (extinction random with respect to taxon age)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extinction of taxa is random with respect to taxon age (the probability of extinction does not decline with age).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Van Valen’s Law as independent empirical support for modeling extinction as effectively random in some respects. Use it to justify null-model assumptions when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonconstructive selectivity / 'wanton extinction'
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass extinction can be selective but not constructive — selective in which taxa are removed, but not constructive in producing organisms better adapted to the 'normal' environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that catastrophic perturbations can change which peculiarities are favored, producing selective extinctions that do not reflect improved adaptation in the usual sense. Label such extinction 'wanton' (selective but not constructive). Expect mass-extinction survivors to be unpredictable based on pre-event adaptedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jablonski’s Law (clade geographic range predicts survivorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: A clade’s (genus/clade) geographic range breadth increases its probability of surviving a mass extinction, independently of the geographic ranges of its constituent species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating survivorship bias during mass extinctions, emphasize clade-level range as a predictor rather than species-level attributes. Note empirical exceptions (e.g., at the end-Cretaceous some patterns—bivalves/gastropods—violate simple species-richness expectations). Use this principle to explain why some clades persist while constituent species’ properties may not predict survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass extinctions require trait-biased stresses (explain higher-order losses)
rubrics_metrics.description: To eliminate many higher-order taxa simultaneously, the extinction-causing stress must 'see' or act upon traits shared by members of those groups (e.g., metabolic rate, size, habitat preference, geographic range).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject pure within-lineage competitive replacement as an explanation for simultaneous loss of distantly related groups; instead search for external stresses that disproportionately affect groups sharing particular traits. Use this criterion to evaluate proposed mass-extinction mechanisms: they must plausibly target shared characteristics across taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass-extinction effects on adaptive topography and subsequent diversification
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass extinctions level adaptive topography—well-adapted taxa before an event may not be favored afterward—thereby opening opportunities for formerly marginal taxa to diversify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret post-extinction adaptive radiations as emergent from the removal of higher taxa and the equilibrium rebound in origination rates. Use extinction-centered explanations (rather than selection-centered) to account for many large-scale diversification events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sepkoski’s kinetic/species-as-particles model for Phanerozoic diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple stochastic/diversification model (species-as-particles) with intrinsic per-taxon diversification rates, equilibria, and stochastic/time-specific perturbations can reproduce large-scale Phanerozoic diversity patterns (Sepkoski Curve).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling long-term diversity, include: (a) intrinsic per-taxon origination and extinction rates toward an equilibrium, (b) slight random components representing environmental perturbations and taxon peculiarities, and (c) time-specific perturbations corresponding to mass-extinction events. Use simulation to test whether complex-looking fossil patterns can arise from a small set of parameters and interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extinction as a central driver of diversification (not merely a by-product)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary models accord extinction (especially mass/wanton extinction) a primary role in generating major adaptive radiations and large-scale diversity patterns, rather than treating extinction as incidental to selection-driven diversification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate hypotheses of diversification by asking whether elevated extinction of higher-order taxa is necessary to achieve observed post-extinction rebound/origination rates. Recognize that random/species-as-particles processes combined with episodic extinctions can produce the sigmoidal, punctuated diversity patterns seen in the fossil record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological principle: use simulations and simple mechanistic models
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer simulations (MBL-style species-as-particles) are a central methodological tool for testing whether proposed evolutionary mechanisms can reproduce fossil-record patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer models that are explicit about assumptions (e.g., independence of species, per-interval probabilities) and that generate testable predictions. Use simulations to reveal whether apparent complexity in the fossil record arises from stochastic dynamics and a few parameters rather than intricate biological detail; avoid overfitting by introducing unnecessary taxon-specific mechanisms unless required by deviations from null simulations.
